passage:
The bus stand was loud and crowded, a horn blaring every few seconds, and Nandini was tired. When the conductor handed over her ticket, her mother Rehana nudged her. "What do we say?"
"Thank you," said Nandini flatly, looking at her shoes.
Rehana did not scold. At the next stop the fruit seller passed a banana up through the window, and Rehana said warmly, "Thank you, that looks so sweet," looking straight at him. Nandini watched.
At the third stop she said it to the seller herself, with no nudge. "Thank you." This time she looked up.

qa.q: Who nudged Nandini to say thank you?
qa.a: Her mother Rehana.

qa.q: How does Nandini feel when she says 'Thank you' to the conductor?
qa.a: Tired and just going through the motions. She says it flatly and looks at her shoes.

qa.q: What choice did Rehana make instead of scolding?
qa.a: She modelled a warm thank you to the fruit seller, looking at him, so Nandini could watch how it is done.

qa.q: What might the fruit seller feel when Nandini says thank you and looks up?
qa.a: Probably pleased and noticed, since the thanks comes with eye contact.

grounding: A child says thank you because she was told to, and repetition and modelling plant the habit before the feeling.

passage:
Every morning Siddharth chirped "Thank you, bhaiya!" to the watchman without breaking stride. It came out like part of the alphabet. His mother Lakshmi noticed he never looked up.
One rainy day she slowed at the gate. "Thank you for holding the umbrella for us, bhaiya. You got wet," she said, and smiled at him. The watchman smiled back and his shoulders eased.
Siddharth stopped skipping. The next morning he said the same words, then glanced up. The watchman waved.
It wasn't feeling yet, just a small peek. Lakshmi went on saying hers aloud.

qa.q: What did Siddharth say to the watchman every morning?
qa.a: 'Thank you, bhaiya!'

qa.q: What does Lakshmi seem to worry about in Siddharth's thank-yous?
qa.a: That they are only a rote phrase with no feeling yet, since he says it like part of the alphabet and never looks up.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do to show Siddharth a different way of saying thanks?
qa.a: She slowed at the gate, named what the watchman had done and smiled at him, letting Siddharth see the effect.

qa.q: How might the watchman feel when Lakshmi thanks him for holding the umbrella?
qa.a: Seen and appreciated, since he smiles back and his shoulders ease.

grounding: A child says thank you as a habit without feeling, and modelling by an adult plants the practice.

passage:
Monday. An aunty gave Gurleen a biscuit. Her mother, Rekha, nudged her. "What do we say?" "Thank you," Gurleen mumbled, already chewing.
Wednesday. At dinner Rekha said, "Thank you for setting the spoons, Gurleen." Papa said, "Thank you for the dal, Rekha." Gurleen watched them.
Saturday. The vegetable man handed Gurleen a free tomato. She looked at it, then up at him. "Thank you," she said, all by herself, and held it like treasure.

qa.q: What did the vegetable man give Gurleen?
qa.a: A free tomato.

qa.q: How did Gurleen seem to feel when she said thank you on Monday?
qa.a: She seemed more interested in the biscuit than grateful, mumbling it only because she was told to.

qa.q: What did Rekha and Papa do that helped the habit grow?
qa.a: They thanked each other and Gurleen at dinner, so she saw thank-you used every day.

qa.q: How might the vegetable man feel when Gurleen thanks him on her own?
qa.a: He'd probably feel pleased and charmed by her unprompted thank-you.

grounding: Shows a child saying thank you on cue before the feeling arrives, and adults' modelling planting the habit.

passage:
Lokesh's birthday party happened in the dark, because the power went out just as the cake came. By candlelight he opened his presents. From Parul Bua there were socks: grey ones, with no dinosaurs.
"Say thank you," whispered his mother.
"Thank you," Lokesh said flatly, dropping them on the floor.
Parul Bua just smiled. Later, when he brought her cake without being asked, she said warmly, "Thank you, Lokesh, that's so kind." He liked how that sounded.
The next week, when his feet were freezing, he pulled on the grey socks. "These are warm," he told his mother, surprised. Then he said thank you again, properly, on the phone to Bua.

qa.q: What did Parul Bua give Lokesh?
qa.a: Grey socks, with no dinosaurs.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when he said "Thank you" flatly?
qa.a: He was disappointed with the plain socks and said it only because he was told to.

qa.q: How did Parul Bua help Lokesh learn real thanks?
qa.a: She didn't scold him; she thanked him warmly for the cake, showing how a real thank-you sounds.

qa.q: How might Parul Bua feel getting Lokesh's phone call?
qa.a: Parul Bua would probably feel touched and happy to hear a thank-you he really meant.

grounding: Shows a child saying thank you only because he is told to, and modelling helping the feeling arrive later.

passage:
Every evening in their Delhi flat, Ganga Dadi folded her hands before dinner and said, "Thank you for this food, and for the hands that made it." Deepak, five, copied her, hands pressed together, eyes open and on the roti. He didn't really know why they did it. He just knew they did.
On Sunday the auto driver dropped them home in the rain and helped carry the shopping to the lift. Dadi thanked him twice. Deepak watched.
That night before dinner, Deepak folded his hands and said, "Thank you for this food, and for the auto uncle who carried the bags." Dadi looked at him, and her eyes went soft.

qa.q: What did Ganga Dadi say before dinner every evening?
qa.a: "Thank you for this food, and for the hands that made it."

qa.q: How did Deepak feel about the ritual at first?
qa.a: He was more interested in the roti; he copied Dadi without really knowing why.

qa.q: What helped Deepak's thank-you become his own?
qa.a: Dadi's steady example every evening, and thanking the auto driver twice, which he watched and then echoed in his own words.

qa.q: What might Dadi feel when her eyes go soft?
qa.a: Dadi probably feels moved and proud that Deepak added his own thank-you.

grounding: Shows a child repeating a thank-you ritual before feeling it, until adult modelling helps it become his own.

passage:
"Himani, what do you say to Dadi for the new frock?"
"...Thank you."
"Nicely, beta."
"Thank you, Dadi," Himani mumbled, already running to try it on.
Later, at dinner, Chetan passed his mother the dal. "Thank you, Amma. It's perfect today."
Himani watched. "Papa, why do you say thank you to Dadi? She's your mummy."
"Because she cooked for us. It makes her happy."
Himani thought about it. When Dadi passed her the papad, she said, "Thank you, Dadi," all by herself, and looked at Papa.
Papa smiled. Dadi smiled more.

qa.q: What did Dadi give Himani?
qa.a: Dadi gave Himani a new frock.

qa.q: What was Himani likely feeling when she mumbled thank you?
qa.a: Himani was excited about the frock and said thanks because she was told to, without really feeling it yet.

qa.q: How did Chetan help the habit of thanks grow?
qa.a: He modelled it himself, thanking Dadi at dinner and explaining it makes her happy, so Himani copied it on her own.

qa.q: How did Dadi feel when Himani thanked her unprompted?
qa.a: Dadi felt pleased and warm, smiling even more than Papa.

grounding: A child says thank you because she is told to, and an adult's modelling plants the habit before the feeling arrives.
